feedback: If pupils equate the frame with the background, contrast the seated class (walker moving) with the pupil walking alongside (walker staying beside them): the background did not change, only the observer's motion did. If pupils cite the class and the background pupil saying 'right' versus 'left', point out that this is a difference in facing direction, not in frame.

For the side-by-side walkers, note that 'the other one looks stationary' (relative speed zero) surfaces the frame idea, whereas 'the same speed as we see them' reflects an absolute-motion assumption to be examined.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference frame is set by the observer's own motion, not by the background or scenery. Observers moving differently (the seated class and the pupil walking alongside) give different but equally valid descriptions of the same walk; observers at rest relative to each other share a frame, even if facing opposite ways makes their left/right words differ.
learnerActions: One pupil stands still to act as 'the background'; the teacher (or another pupil) walks steadily between that pupil and the class, while a second pupil walks alongside the walker at the same pace as a moving observer.

The seated class describes the walker as moving across the room; the moving observer describes the walker as staying beside them. The background pupil may say 'to the left' where the class says 'to the right' only because they face the other way: they are at rest relative to the class, so they share the class's frame and agree the walker is moving at the same speed.
Compare the two descriptions of the exact same walk and discuss why they differ.
State explicitly that the reference frame is set by the observer's own motion, not by the background pupil, the scenery, or which way the observer is facing.
Extend: walk two pupils side by side at the same steady pace and have the class predict how fast each walker sees the OTHER moving, and why, before asking the walkers.
activities.title: Walk-across-the-room: viewpoint vs background

feedback: If a learner always adds the two speeds, test their rule on the same-speed same-direction case: adding would give double the speed, but the correct relative speed is zero because they appear stationary to each other — so same direction must subtract.
For the oncoming pair at 50 and 40, confirm the closing speed is 50 + 40 = 90; for the same-direction pair, the difference is 50 − 40 = 10.
Always ask which object the relative speed is measured relative to, so the number is tied to a frame.
activities.intendedInsight: Relative speed is found by subtracting the speeds when objects move the same way and adding them when they move towards or away from each other in opposite directions; the same-speed same-direction case gives zero relative speed (appears stationary).
learnerActions: Work through the same-direction case: two trains (or cars) travelling the same way at the same speed — compute the relative speed and confirm it is zero, so each appears stationary to the other.
Work through two cars driving side by side at the same 60 mph: state how fast each appears to move as seen from the other, and explain why it looks stationary.

Work through an oncoming case: two cars approach each other, one at 50 and one at 40 — compute how fast they close on each other (50 + 40 = 90), then redo it for both going the same way (50 − 40 = 10, closing if the faster is behind or separating if it is ahead).

Optionally use a number line: mark where each car is after one hour from where they started. In opposite directions the distance between them changes by both distances together (50 + 40 = 90), while in the same direction it changes only by the difference (50 − 40 = 10).
State the rule in your own words: same direction → subtract the speeds; towards or away in opposite directions → add the speeds.
Name the frame for each answer (e.g. 'relative to the other car').
activities.title: Compute relative speed: add or subtract?

feedback: If a learner insists one train is 'really' moving regardless of frame, have them re-tell the scene from each frame so each train becomes 'the mover', and require the frame to be named every time.
If a learner reads the motion off the background scenery, strip the scenery away (two trains, no visible ground) to show the motion is symmetric.

If a learner tries to resolve the ambiguity by calling one view 'real' and the other 'just an optical illusion', clarify that neither description is a mere illusion: both are equally valid relative to their frames, so the fix is to name the frame, not to decide which view is the real motion.

Use the steady-straight-line train question to surface that, for steady straight-line motion and without an outside reference, no internal observation singles out one frame as 'truly' moving; changes in speed or direction can be felt, which is a separate idea.
activities.intendedInsight: Looking only at the other train, your train going forwards and their train going backwards look identical — the view is genuinely ambiguous. There is no single 'really moving' answer without saying relative to what.
learnerActions: Consider: two trains sit side by side at a platform; yours begins to move smoothly, and looking only out of the window at the other train, it seems as though the OTHER train is sliding backwards.
Explain how the same view can mean either 'we are moving' or 'they are moving', and what decides which is true.
Resolve the ambiguity by naming a frame: relative to the platform/ground, whichever train's position changes is the mover; relative to the other train, each sees the other move.
Answer a paired question from two frames: 'You're on the train — is the platform moving?' answered from the train's frame AND from the platform's frame.

Discuss: is there any experiment inside a train moving at a steady speed in a straight line that could tell you you're moving, without looking outside? (Speeding up, braking or going round a bend can be felt, so keep the question to steady straight-line motion.)
activities.title: The ambiguous two-train departure
